The Big Three: Head to Head

BMW, KTM, and Triumph dominate the large adventure bike market. Each offers a distinct interpretation of the adventure touring concept, and choosing between them is one of the most debated topics in British biking. We put all three through their paces on a week-long Scottish tour to settle the argument.

BMW R 1300 GS

The GS needs no introduction. The R 1300 brings a new chassis, revised boxer engine with 143bhp, and the most comprehensive electronics suite in the class. The new EVO Telelever front suspension improves feel over the previous generation, and the optional adaptive ride height lowers the seat at stops. On tour, the GS is supremely comfortable with outstanding wind protection and a vast range of factory accessories. It is the complete package but also the most expensive at over eighteen thousand pounds before options.

KTM 1390 Super Adventure S

KTM takes the performance approach. The 1350cc V-twin produces a class-leading 173bhp with sharper throttle response than either rival. The WP semi-active suspension is outstanding, and the electronics package rivals the BMW for sophistication. On road, the KTM is the sportiest — it encourages you to ride faster and harder than the others. The trade-off is a slightly less refined touring experience. Wind noise is higher and the seat is firmer for long days.

Triumph Tiger 1200 Rally Pro

Triumph's triple-cylinder engine is the character star. The 1160cc triple delivers a distinctive exhaust note and addictive mid-range punch that makes every overtake a pleasure. Shaft drive eliminates chain maintenance entirely, and the semi-active suspension handles weight changes smoothly. The Tiger is slightly lighter than the GS and narrower, making it more manageable in tight situations.

Comparison Table

  • Power: BMW 143bhp | KTM 173bhp | Triumph 148bhp
  • Weight: BMW 237kg | KTM 238kg | Triumph 230kg
  • Tank: BMW 19.5L | KTM 23L | Triumph 20L
  • Drive: BMW shaft | KTM chain | Triumph shaft
  • Price: BMW from 18K | KTM from 17.5K | Triumph from 17K

The Verdict

Choose the BMW if you want the most complete touring package with the widest range of accessories and the best dealer network across the UK.

Choose the KTM if performance and sportiness matter more than comfort, and you enjoy pushing the pace on twisty roads.

Choose the Triumph if engine character, shaft drive convenience, and British heritage appeal. It is arguably the best all-rounder of the three. All three are superb touring machines. You would not be disappointed with any of them. The differences are subtle — test ride all three and let your gut feeling guide the decision.
keyTakeaways: BMW, KTM and Triumph offer distinct takes on the large adventure bike concept.
The KTM 1390 leads on power with 173bhp, the sportiest of the three.
The Triumph Tiger 1200 is lightest at 230kg and uses convenient shaft drive.
The BMW R 1300 GS has the widest accessory range and best UK dealer network.
All three are superb, so test ride each and let feel guide the decision.

faq.q: Which of the big three should I choose?
faq.a: Choose the BMW R 1300 GS for the most complete package, widest accessories and best UK dealer network. Choose the KTM 1390 if performance and sportiness matter most. Choose the Triumph Tiger 1200 for engine character, shaft-drive convenience and arguably the best all-round balance.

faq.q: Is shaft drive an advantage here?
faq.a: Both the BMW and Triumph use shaft drive, eliminating chain maintenance entirely over a tour, while the KTM uses a chain. On a week away, shaft drive removes cleaning, lubing and adjustment, which is a genuine convenience, though the KTM's chain keeps weight and complexity down.

The Triumph Tiger 1200 is slightly lighter at 230kg and narrower than the GS, making it more manageable in tight situations. All three sit within 8kg of each other, so seat height, ergonomics and how the bike carries its weight matter more than the headline figure.

faq.q: Does the KTM's extra power matter on UK roads?
faq.a: The KTM's 173bhp is the most in class and it feels the sportiest, encouraging you to ride harder. On British roads that performance is rarely fully usable, and the trade-off is higher wind noise and a firmer seat, so the calmer BMW or Triumph may suit longer tours better.
